title: Macros you'll read
intro: A macro is code that writes code. The compiler runs it, puts what it produced where the call was, and only then checks types. You met the macros you call every day in [Macros, attributes and naming](/learn/macros-attributes-naming/). This page is for reading the others: a `macro_rules!` block in a dependency, a `#[derive(...)]` that writes code you never see, an attribute such as `#[tokio::main]`. You will read far more macros than you write.

coming_from.go: Go has no macros. `map[string]int{...}` is syntax the language provides. Rust has no map literal, and the `hashmap!` macro below fills the gap. `go generate` is the nearest idea: it runs a program you wrote and leaves source files behind. A Rust macro runs inside the compiler whenever the crate is compiled and leaves nothing in your source tree.
coming_from.kotlin: Kotlin has no macros either: `mapOf("a" to 1)` is an ordinary function. Code generators for Kotlin, such as KSP, are compiler plugins. Rust's derive and attribute macros fill that role, and the ones you add yourself (serde's, for example) arrive as a crate in `Cargo.toml`.
coming_from.python: Python has no macro stage: ordinary code cannot rewrite other code before it runs. `@dataclass` rewrites a class when the module is imported; `#[derive]` writes its code while the program compiles, so a mistake is reported before anything runs.
coming_from.typescript: TypeScript has no macros. A Babel plugin is the nearest mechanism: it rewrites code in a build step, outside the language, for the whole build. Decorators run when the program runs. A Rust macro is part of the compiler's own pipeline and runs only where the code names it.
coming_from.java: An annotation is metadata, and an annotation processor reads it inside `javac` while your code compiles and generates code. `#[derive]` and attribute macros are the nearest match, and `macro_rules!` has no Java counterpart at all.
coming_from.csharp: A source generator runs inside the C# compiler and adds code, as a derive macro does. A `macro_rules!` macro has no C# counterpart, and `[CallerArgumentExpression]` covers one small job macros do, capturing the text of an argument.
coming_from.c: A `#define` substitutes tokens before the compiler parses anything, which is where `SQUARE(x) x*x` goes wrong. `macro_rules!` works on parsed pieces of code (an `expr`, a `ty`), and the variables a macro makes do not collide with yours.
coming_from.cpp: Templates and `constexpr` do much of what you would reach for a macro to do, and Rust's generics do the same jobs. What templates cannot do (generate a function whose name you pass in, capture an expression's text) is the work of macros.

notes: A name followed by `!` is a macro call, and it may use `()`, `[]` or `{}`. The rules of the macro decide what may go inside, so `vec![1, 2]` and `hashmap! { "a" => 1 }` are different grammars.
`macro_rules!` is a list of rules, each `(pattern) => { code }`. To read a call, find the first rule whose pattern fits, then swap the pieces the pattern captured into the code.
`$x:expr` captures one expression, `$name:ident` a name, `$t:ty` a type, and `$( ... ),*` repeats whatever is inside it, separated by commas.
Derives and attributes such as `#[tokio::main]` are macros too. Those from a crate are Rust functions that read and write tokens, in a crate of their own.
A function is the right tool until it is not. A macro is for what a function cannot do: take a list of any length, generate items, capture the text of an expression.

gotcha.title: A macro call has the syntax its author gave it
gotcha.looks_fine: In Python, TypeScript and Go, `"Ada": 36` is how an entry of a map or object is written. A macro that builds a map might be expected to accept the same.
gotcha.rust_sees: `hashmap!` is not part of the language. It has one rule, and that rule says each pair is `key => value`. A `:` fits no rule, so the compiler stops at it.
gotcha.why: The macro's own patterns decide what a call may look like. The error names the token that fits no rule and points at what the macro was trying to match when it gave up. When you meet a macro you do not know, its documentation or its `macro_rules!` block is where the grammar is written.

go.says: Go runs this. A map literal is part of the language, and `key: value` is how its entries are written.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this, but the pairs are written `"Ada" to 36`: `mapOf` is a function and `to` makes a pair. There is no colon form.

python.says: Python runs this. A dict literal is part of the language, with the colon.

typescript.says: TypeScript runs this. An object literal takes `key: value`. A `Map` has no literal and takes an array of pairs instead.
typescript.code:
const ages = { Ada: 36, Linus: 28 };
console.log("entries:", Object.keys(ages).length);

java.says: Java runs this, with `Map.of("Ada", 36, ...)`, an ordinary method that takes keys and values in turn. Java has no map literal.

csharp.says: C# runs this. A collection initializer is part of the language and takes `["Ada"] = 36` entries.
csharp.code:
var ages = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["Ada"] = 36, ["Linus"] = 28 };
Console.WriteLine($"entries: {ages.Count}");

c.says: C runs this, with an array of structs: the standard library has no map type to write a literal for.

cpp.says: C++ runs this. A `std::map` takes a list of `{key, value}` pairs through an initializer list.

dataclass.py.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
import inspect


def announce(cls):
    print("decorator runs for", cls.__name__)
    return cls


print("before the class statement")


@announce
@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int


print("after the class statement")
print("generated __init__:", inspect.signature(Point.__init__))
print("generated __repr__:", Point(1, 2))
